issues: The statement merges two separate rules in Bava Batra 3:7 and pins the privacy gloss on the wrong one. The Mishnah (a) bars a partner from opening new windows into a jointly owned courtyard, and (b) bars opening 'an entrance opposite another entrance or a window opposite another window toward a courtyard belonging to partners'. The translator's gloss 'so as to ensure that the residents will enjoy a measure of privacy' is attached to (b), not to a general ban on windows or doorways 'facing' the courtyard.

The quotes are verbatim, and the source note correctly marks the privacy clause as the Koren/Steinsaltz translator's unbolded interpolation. The dating context (c. 200 CE) is consistent with the standard account that Judah ha-Nasi compiled the Mishnah in the late 2nd or early 3rd century. The note's claim about hezek re'iyah in Bava Batra 2b is also correct: the Sefaria Davidson English for Bava Batra 2b discusses 'whether damage caused by sight is called damage'.

fieldFixes.statement: The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code (compiled c. 200 CE), bars a person from opening new windows into a courtyard he shares with partners, and from opening a doorway opposite a neighbour's doorway or a window opposite a neighbour's window onto such a courtyard - a rule a modern English translation glosses as ensuring residents 'a measure of privacy'.

Re-fetched: FOUND. The clause directly follows the bold Mishnah words 'A person may not open an entrance opposite [another] entrance or a window opposite [another] window toward a courtyard belonging to partners'. It is the translator's unbolded explanation and glosses that rule specifically.

issues: The source note says 'The same passage limits the principle: sheriffs could still enter...'. That is inaccurate. The OLL extract quoted does not mention sheriffs; the knock-and-announce limit is a separate resolution in the report (5 Co. Rep. 91b), which OLL describes only in its editorial 'Thoughts'.

The OLL page wrongly calls Coke 'the English judge' who 'declared in a ruling'. In 1604 Coke was Attorney General and only reported the case; the judges were Popham CJ and others of the King's Bench. The record's 'reported by Sir Edward Coke' is correct, but the cited page does not support it, so an independent source has been added.
Date: 1604 (Michaelmas Term) is standard. Note that the U.S. Supreme Court in Wilson v. Arkansas (1995) cites 'K.B.1603', so some U.S. sources date it 1603.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched with the cache cleared: quote FOUND verbatim in the OLL extract, 'Found in: Selected Writings of Sir Edward Coke, vol. I' (Liberty Fund, ed. Sheppard, 2003). Semayne's Case, 5 Co. Rep. 91a, 77 Eng. Rep. 194 (K.B., Michaelmas Term 1604). Coke, then Attorney General, reported the case; OLL's own commentary wrongly calls him the judge. The quoted passage does not contain the sheriff limit. That limit is a separate resolution in the report (5 Co. Rep. 91b): 'when the King is party, the sheriff (if the doors be not open) may break the party's house' after he 'ought to signify the cause of his coming'.

issues: 'often with tamper-evident locks' overstates the source. The paper says only 'We observe built-in tamper-evident locking mechanisms' and assigns letterlocking formats a range of security scores; it does not say such locks were common. This is softened to 'some with'.

fieldFixes.statement: Before mass-produced envelopes spread in the 1830s, most letters were 'letterlocked' - folded and secured to become their own envelopes, some with built-in tamper-evident locks; a European postmaster's trunk of 300-year-old undelivered post, the Brienne Collection, contained 577 letterpackets that had never been opened when researchers catalogued it for a 2021 study.

issues: 'held' overstates it. The Court denied Jackson's petition and upheld his conviction under the ban on mailing lottery circulars (the opinion ends 'Denied.'). The sealed-letters passage is Justice Field's statement of the Fourth Amendment limit on postal power. Later courts often cite it as a holding, but in the case itself it is a declaration made while upholding the mail ban. The corrected text says so and adds the decision date.
Date: 'October Term 1877' is correct (the LII page shows it). CourtListener's API gives dateFiled 1878-05-13 (also '1877 U.S. LEXIS 1718'), so 1878 is the decision year.

fieldFixes.statement: In Ex parte Jackson (96 U.S. 727, October Term 1877, decided May 1878), the U.S. Supreme Court - while upholding a ban on mailing lottery circulars - declared that sealed letters in the mail are as protected from inspection 'as if they were retained by the parties forwarding them in their own domiciles', and may be opened only under a warrant - carrying the protection of the home to the sealed page.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched with the cache cleared: quote FOUND verbatim in Justice Field's opinion for the Court. The next sentences say such letters 'can only be opened and examined under like warrant ... as is required when papers are subjected to search in one's own household', which supports the 'home' framing. The page header reads '96 U.S. 727 / 24 L.Ed. 877 / October Term, 1877'. The disposition at the end is 'Denied.' Decision date 1878-05-13 is from the CourtListener API; courtlistener.com HTML pages return a JS challenge to scripts.
